title: A Field Guide to AI Market Freakouts
dek: One extended theme today: the latest China-driven AI selloff. NLW zooms out to catalog every recurring way investors panic about AI — cheap models, circular financing, revenue-vs-CapEx, token caps, scaling walls — and argues the market's compulsive bubble-hunting is exactly what keeps a real bubble from forming.

oneIdea.headline: AI market freakouts follow a pattern — and the pattern is why the bubble hasn't formed.
oneIdea.summary: Since ChatGPT, investors have cycled through the same anxieties: cheap Chinese models, circular financing, revenue not justifying spend, CapEx running too hot, token caps, scaling walls. NLW's field guide walks each one, notes they often coincide with predictable summer seasonality, and lands on a counterintuitive conclusion — the market's relentless determination to call everything a bubble is itself the pressure-release valve keeping a runaway 1999-style bubble from ever taking hold.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Whether it is a bubble or not, do not bet the surgery on the cheapest tool
items.body: The whole edition is an argument about AI's finances, and the two camps disagree completely. If Zitron is right that the build-out is a debt-funded bubble propped up by two loss-making labs, then some of today's AI clinical tools are being sold below cost and a shake-out could see prices jump, features withdrawn, or a supplier fold. If NLW is right that the market simply overreacts and the sector grows steadily, the risk is milder but not zero. Either way the practical instruction for a practice is the same: when choosing an AI scribe or triage tool, favour a supplier likely to be solvent in three years, read the exit terms, and make sure patient records and letters can be exported if the product disappears.

items.title: Concentration risk applies to clinical suppliers too
items.body: Zitron's central claim is that almost all AI demand traces back to a handful of firms and their backers. Most AI scribes and triage products are thin wrappers over a model from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or a Chinese lab. If NLW is right, that is fine and the models keep improving. If Zitron is right, a wobble at one lab could degrade or interrupt a tool a surgery has come to depend on mid-clinic. It is a fair due-diligence question to ask any vendor which model sits underneath, and what happens to your service if that provider raises prices sharply or pulls access.

items.title: The honest healthcare read: this is a money story, not a safety story
items.body: Unlike some editions, there is little direct clinical content here. The value for general practice is disposition, not diagnosis: do not over-commit to long contracts or expensive integrations on the assumption that today's generous pricing is permanent, and keep any AI tool as an assistant with a clinician in the loop, so that a commercial collapse upstream is an inconvenience rather than a clinical risk.

the_other_side.text: Where NLW argues the market's relentless bubble-hunting is a pressure-release valve, that circular financing is nothing like the dot-com trap because OpenAI pays cash for GPUs, and that cancelled data centres reflect hard construction rather than weak demand, Zitron's argument is the mirror image. He contends the AI build-out is a genuine debt-funded asset bubble whose special-purpose vehicles are the equivalent of 2008's collateralised debt obligations: off-balance-sheet structures, reminiscent of Enron, that hide something like 1.65 trillion dollars of obligations while NVIDIA finances the very companies buying its chips and then rents that capacity back. He estimates that 70 to 90 percent of compute demand comes from OpenAI and Anthropic, two loss-making firms, and that roughly fifteen times more data-centre capacity is being built than real demand supports. On his reading the freakouts are not preventing a bubble; they are belatedly noticing a real one.

the_truth_beneath.text: The single variable both men orbit is whether demand for AI compute is real and durable enough to service the debt now being raised against it. Both accept the facts of scale: staggering capital spending heading past a trillion dollars, roughly half the S&P 500 AI-exposed, and much of the financing routed through hyperscalers and neoclouds. The empirical question that will resolve is whether paying customers exist beyond OpenAI and Anthropic to fill the capacity, and whether those two can keep paying. The observable that settles it is third-party compute revenue and remaining performance obligations from buyers who are not hyperscalers or the two big labs, plus whether the data-centre SPVs actually meet their debt-service ratios once leases begin. The residue is worldview: NLW reads compulsive bubble-calling as self-correcting; Zitron reads it as recognition of hidden systemic leverage. NLW is vindicated if diverse enterprise demand climbs to absorb the build and spending keeps being funded without defaults; Zitron if demand stays concentrated in two unprofitable labs and the SPVs start missing payments. Both are polemicists with incentives, NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype, so the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: both concede the spending is enormous and both concede it currently hinges on two loss-making companies. Watch whether compute revenue from anyone other than OpenAI, Anthropic and their hyperscaler backers actually materialises.

headlines.headline: Treasury floats sanctions over distillation attacks
headlines.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed that Chinese AI companies could face sanctions and entity-list designations as a response to 'covert industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft.' It's the first time an executive-branch member suggested the government might actually act on distillation.

headlines.headline: White House accuses Moonshot of distilling Anthropic's Fable
headlines.summary: OSTP Director Michael Kratsios alleged Moonshot built 'a sophisticated internal platform to conduct large-scale distillation against US models' for its K3 model, switching between access methods to avoid detection, and accessed GB300 servers in Thailand. Anthropic confirmed it's working with the administration on the matter.

headlines.headline: Congratulations, you protected domestic AI companies by taxing the competitiveness of the entire country.
headlines.attribution: Signal, on the proposed China AI restrictions
headlines.summary: Signal's viral summary argued the crackdown forces US companies to buy pricier American AI while the rest of the world uses cheaper models of equal intelligence — and distillation doesn't stop just because Washington publishes a list.

headlines.headline: The White House is split on how to fight Chinese AI
headlines.summary: Per Wired, parts of the White House want stricter controls while Commerce sees them as unworkable. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reportedly favors combating Chinese AI with competition — pitching direct incentives for US labs to open-source their models rather than regulating anyone.

headlines.headline: AI is now 25% of US GDP growth
headlines.summary: Per Bloomberg, AI investment represents 25% of US GDP growth — the largest single-sector contribution in history. JPMorgan credits AI with 75% of S&P 500 returns, 80% of earnings growth, and 90% of capital-spending growth since ChatGPT's release.

headlines.headline: Even passive indexers are making a bet on AI
headlines.summary: With roughly 50% of the S&P 500 now AI or AI-exposed, NLW argues everyone needs to understand the narrative — even a 401(k) contributor or passive indexer carries significant AI exposure whether they realize it or not.

headlines.headline: The 'cheap models' freakout is a DeepSeek rerun
headlines.summary: This round echoes the early-2025 DeepSeek panic, when markets believed a Chinese lab built frontier AI for a few million dollars. Investors later learned the difference between training and inference compute — and that R1 wasn't actually ahead, just the first free reasoning model.

headlines.headline: Kimi K3 is cheaper — but not pennies on the dollar
headlines.summary: K3 is being served at around a third of Fable's price or half of Opus — a meaningful saving, but far from the near-free clone many analysts imagine. The 'Chinese AI is cheap, US AI is eye-watering' framing is oversimplified.

headlines.headline: Circular financing isn't the dot-com trap people fear
headlines.summary: The worry that Nvidia's investments flow straight back as chip revenue misreads history: unlike Cisco's 1990s vendor financing, OpenAI pays cash for GPUs. If OpenAI stumbles, Nvidia holds devalued stock, not a debt default and a balance-sheet hole.

headlines.headline: Google found Wall Street's AI spending limit: $200B
headlines.summary: Google posted 24% overall growth and 82% cloud growth — but the stock fell 1.2% because CapEx guidance hit $200 billion. 'The two hundred was the do-not-cross line,' said Zacks' Brian Mulberry, likely the psychological shock of a round number more than the fundamentals.

headlines.headline: Combined CapEx is heading past $1 trillion next year
headlines.summary: Hyperscalers have raised CapEx guidance every quarter for three years, with combined spend on track to exceed a trillion dollars in 2027. The flip side of 'revenue not growing fast enough' is 'CapEx growing too fast' — the bigger the spend, the steeper the revenue hill.

headlines.headline: Agentic spend broke the seat-based revenue math
headlines.summary: Late-2025 bubble talk faded when analysts stopped multiplying knowledge-worker seats by $20-30 and saw agentic use cases arrive — employees spending hundreds or thousands per month. It made clear AI isn't just another category of SaaS.

headlines.headline: That MIT '95% of pilots fail' study was garbage science
headlines.summary: NLW dismisses the notorious report as 'absolute garbage social science MIT should be embarrassed to be associated with' — but notes it didn't matter, because the headline landed on every Wall Street desk anyway.

headlines.headline: Token caps are less dramatic than the headlines
headlines.summary: Uber caps users at $1,500/month and Tesla allows $200/week with the ability to request more. Since most knowledge workers use nowhere near those budgets, even universal adoption of such policies leaves enormous room for growth.

headlines.headline: The 2024 'scaling wall' fear now looks ridiculous
headlines.summary: Fall-2024 panic held that pre-training had plateaued and both labs scuttled flagship runs. Then o1 revealed reasoning as a new performance vector, and pre-training clearly didn't hit a wall — few would argue Fable V isn't a completely different beast from Opus III.

headlines.headline: AI FUD has a seasonality — investors want an August excuse
headlines.summary: Summer momentum breakdowns are well documented, especially when semis drive the rally. Morgan Stanley notes momentum stocks are down 40% this month — the worst on record, beating early-2021's 29% — while Goldman says hedge funds sold tech in record numbers.

headlines.headline: The market's bubble obsession is what prevents a bubble
headlines.summary: NLW argues that a generation raised on The Big Short calling everything a bubble is a feature, not a bug: every time the market gets over its skis, there's a pressure release. We're not seeing the frenetic 1999-2000 boom-and-bust IPO frenzy.

headlines.headline: Data centers are too slow to build to overshoot demand
headlines.summary: Half of this year's announced data centers were canceled or delayed — which bears read as weak demand, but NLW says the simpler explanation is that permitting and construction are genuinely hard and builders have badly mishandled community concerns. These road bumps buy the economy time to adjust.

headlines.headline: Cheap models don't matter if you can't serve them
headlines.summary: NLW argues this China round resolves once people realize inference capacity matters more than price: Moonshot was completely tapped out of compute on K3's opening weekend, and it's questionable whether all Chinese labs combined can serve even a fraction of US companies' users.

headlines.headline: The US government does not owe either of the large labs a business model.
headlines.summary: Investor Nick Carter argued that if token economics collapse, American enterprise will be fine — benefiting from hyper-deflation in the cost of cognition. The hyperscalers, neoclouds and internet companies survive; only OpenAI and Anthropic's current forms are at risk, and they can adapt.

headlines.headline: NLW's base case: frontier tokens sell at a premium for five years
headlines.summary: He expects every frontier token to be bought at a premium for at least five years even as cheaper workloads come online, because premium state-of-the-art supply stays ahead of demand. A flourishing of routers, fine-tuning and vertical model plays distributes AI's revenue gains and relieves pressure on the big two labs to carry the whole market.
